trial_name: 6S — Hydroxyethyl Starch 130/0.42 vs Ringer's Acetate in Severe Sepsis (2012)
citation: Perner A, Haase N, Guttormsen AB, et al. Hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.42 versus Ringer's acetate in severe sepsis. N Engl J Med. 2012;367(2):124-134.
trial_type: RCT — investigator-initiated, multicentre, parallel-group, double-blind, superiority
one_liner: Resuscitation with 6% HES 130/0.42 significantly increased 90-day mortality and renal replacement therapy compared to Ringer's acetate in severe sepsis.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients (aged 18 or older) with severe sepsis within the prior 24 hours requiring fluid resuscitation.
pico.intervention: 6% Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) 130/0.42 in a balanced electrolyte solution (capped at 33 mL/kg ideal body weight/day).
pico.comparison: Ringer's acetate balanced crystalloid (capped at same daily dose; open-label Ringer's permitted beyond cap).
pico.outcome: Composite of all-cause mortality or dialysis dependence at 90 days.

background.existing_knowledge: Hydroxyethyl starch solutions were widely used in sepsis for volume expansion based on perceived hemodynamic efficiency compared to crystalloids.
background.knowledge_gap: Older starch formulations caused renal impairment and coagulopathy, but whether newer, low-molecular-weight tetrastarches (HES 130/0.42) were safer in severe sepsis remained controversial.
background.hypothesis: Resuscitation with 6% HES 130/0.42 in a balanced carrier solution reduces 90-day mortality or dialysis dependence compared with Ringer's acetate in severe sepsis.

methods.design: Multicenter, double-blind, randomized, parallel-group trial with stratified randomization by presence of shock, hematological malignancy, and hospital type (university vs non-university).
methods.setting: 26 ICUs across Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden.

inclusion: Adults aged 18 years or older in ICU
Fulfilled severe sepsis criteria within the previous 24 hours
Clinically judged to require intravascular volume expansion
exclusion: Receipt of >1000 mL synthetic colloid in the 24 hours pre-randomization
Conditions where trial fluid was considered unsafe or inappropriate

methods.intervention: 6% HES 130/0.42 in a balanced carrier solution as the primary resuscitation fluid. Capped at 33 mL/kg ideal body weight/day; open-label Ringer's acetate permitted if cap reached. Permanently stopped if RRT initiated or severe adverse reaction occurred.
methods.comparison: Ringer's acetate as the primary resuscitation fluid, capped at 33 mL/kg ideal body weight/day to maintain blinding; open-label Ringer's acetate permitted beyond cap.
methods.blinding: Double-blind using identical masked fluid containers; clinicians, patients, investigators, and outcome assessors were blinded.
methods.sample_size_power: 800 patients planned to detect a 10% absolute reduction in primary outcome (50% to 40%) with 80% power at alpha 0.05, assuming 45% mortality and 5% dialysis dependence.
methods.primary_outcome: Composite of death or dialysis dependence at 90 days post-randomization.
secondary_outcomes: Renal replacement therapy use up to day 90

headline_bullets: HES 130/0.42 significantly increased 90-day mortality (51% vs 43%, P=0.03).
HES 130/0.42 significantly increased the requirement for renal replacement therapy (22% vs 16%, P=0.04).
Bleeding risks and blood product transfusions were significantly higher in the HES group.
Total trial fluid administered was identical between groups (median 3000 mL vs 3000 mL, P=0.20).

outcomes_table.outcome: Primary composite: death or dialysis dependence at day 90
Renal replacement therapy (any use to day 90)

outcomes_table.note: Missing data for 1 participant in Ringer's group

outcomes_table.outcome: Doubling of plasma creatinine OR RRT (post-hoc)
Mean % days alive without RRT up to day 90
Mean % days alive and out of hospital up to day 90
Cumulative trial fluid in ICU (mL, median [IQR])

outcomes_table.note: Includes packed red cells, plasma, and platelets

subgroup_table.subgroup: Acute kidney injury at randomisation — Yes
Acute kidney injury at randomisation — No

safety: Increased 90-day all-cause mortality with HES 130/0.42 (51% vs 43%, RR 1.17, P=0.03)
Increased requirement for renal replacement therapy with HES 130/0.42 (22% vs 16%, RR 1.35, P=0.04)
Increased rate of any bleeding event in ICU with HES (23% vs 15%, P=0.003)
Higher volume of blood products transfused in HES group (median 1340 vs 1055 mL, P=0.003)
Severe bleeding in ICU: 10% in HES vs 6% in Ringer's (RR 1.52, 95% CI 0.94–2.48, P=0.09)
Severe allergic reaction in ICU: 0.3% in HES vs 0% in Ringer's (P=0.32)

domains.notes: Central stratified randomization ensured good allocation concealment and baseline group balance.
Double-blind design using identical masked fluid bags successfully minimized performance and outcome detection bias.
804 randomized, 798 analyzed in modified ITT (received >=1 dose of fluid); 90-day primary outcome follow-up was complete.

Daily cap exceeded in 28 HES vs 41 Ringer's patients. Non-trial synthetic colloids given post-randomization to 39 HES vs 38 Ringer's patients. 42% in each group received synthetic colloids in 24 hours pre-randomization (median 700 vs 500 mL).
Well balanced: median SAPS II 50 vs 52, SOFA 9 vs 9, shock present in 84% vs 84%, kidney injury present in 36% vs 35%, median time from admission to randomization 3.7 vs 4.0 hours.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is high, supported by double-blinding, complete follow-up, and balanced groups, though unprotocolized RRT triggers add minor variability.

domains.notes: Enrolled critically ill adults with severe sepsis and high disease severity (84% shock) across 26 Scandinavian ICUs.
Directly applicable to ICU fluid resuscitation in sepsis, but less applicable to pre-ICU resuscitation or non-septic patient populations.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for adult ICU patients with severe sepsis and septic shock in developed healthcare systems.

strengths: Large, double-blind, multicenter RCT comparing modern tetrastarch to balanced crystalloid
Pragmatic design evaluating patient-centered, hard outcomes at 90 days
High baseline balance and complete primary outcome follow-up
Equal volume of trial fluid administered between groups, isolating fluid type as the causal exposure
limitations: Modified intention-to-treat design excluded 6 randomized patients who received no trial fluid
Initiation thresholds for RRT were determined by treating clinicians rather than strict protocolized criteria
Pre-randomization exposure to synthetic colloids in 42% of patients may have blunted baseline separation
Composite outcome primary driver was mortality, as 90-day dialysis dependence was rare (1 patient per group)

critical_appraisal.summary: High-quality, double-blind RCT demonstrating clear clinical harm (increased 90-day mortality and RRT) from HES 130/0.42 compared to balanced crystalloid in severe sepsis.
strengths: Use of balanced crystalloid comparator rather than saline
Clear isolation of toxicity independent of total fluid volume
weaknesses: Lack of standardized criteria for RRT initiation
High rates of pre-randomization colloid administration

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients with severe sepsis, resuscitation with 6% HES 130/0.42 significantly increased 90-day mortality and the need for renal replacement therapy compared with Ringer's acetate.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Do not use hydroxyethyl starch solutions for fluid resuscitation in patients with sepsis or septic shock; use crystalloids.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients requiring volume expansion for severe sepsis or septic shock.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Early hemodynamic goals were non-beneficial; hemodynamic surrogates (lactate 2.2 vs 2.2 mmol/L at 0-12h) appeared similar despite diverging long-term clinical harms.
implementation_caveats: Total fluid balance during ICU stay was similar (median 5452 vs 4616 mL, P=0.17)
Toxicity occurs even within recommended daily dosing limits (33 mL/kg/day)

controversies.notes: Critics argued RRT timing depended on clinician preference, but concordance with the objective mortality signal reinforced genuine renal harm.
Lactate values (0-12h 2.2 vs 2.2 mmol/L; 12-24h 2.0 vs 2.0 mmol/L) were identical, demonstrating that early surrogate targets fail to reflect delayed organ toxicity.

context_related_trials.relation: Subsequent large ICU RCT in a broader population that confirmed increased RRT requirement with HES 130/0.42 and no survival advantage over saline.

unresolved_questions: Whether non-septic surgical or trauma populations experience the same risk of renal toxicity and mortality from low-substitution starches.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.42 causes increased mortality and renal failure in severe sepsis and should be avoided in favor of balanced crystalloids.
